title: Are We Alone?
intro_sentence: Thousands of worlds later, the oldest question is closer to a test than ever — but honesty about what we do and don't know is the whole discipline.
narrative_101: The exoplanet count now runs into the thousands, and statistics say roughly every star hosts planets, with small rocky worlds in habitable zones numbering in the billions across the galaxy. The stage for life, at least, is vast.
That's what makes the silence loud. If habitable real estate is everywhere, where is everyone? — the question Enrico Fermi framed over lunch, still unanswered.
We have gone from 'are there other worlds?' — settled, yes — to 'are any of them alive?', a question we can finally start to test rather than only argue about.
body_paragraphs: The Drake equation frames the odds as a chain of factors — how many stars, how many with planets, how many habitable, how many that develop life, and so on. Exoplanet science has now pinned the first factors observationally: planets are common, and habitable-zone rocky worlds abundant. The later factors remain unknown.

The next step is empirical, not philosophical. Reading the atmospheres of temperate rocky worlds for biosignatures — patiently, with instruments and standards built to survive scrutiny — is how the question moves from the Drake equation's guesses toward a measurement.

The honest state of the art: no life beyond Earth has been detected, no biosignature confirmed. But for the first time, the tools to look are real — and that is the quiet revolution the exoplanet era has delivered.

We have not only listened but spoken. In 1974 the Arecibo radio telescope beamed a three-minute pictogram toward the globular cluster M13, 25,000 light-years away, and in 1977 both Voyager spacecraft left Earth carrying the Golden Record — greetings, music, and images bolted to a probe now drifting between the stars. Both are gestures more than conversations, but they are humanity's first deliberate messages to whoever might be out there.
